- When sentiment is high (≥0.7) and forecast is trending up, reduce peak overshoots by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to bullish sentiment.
- When sentiment is low (≤0.3) and forecast is trending down, avoid excessive downward corrections — model should not dip below 1–2% below recent low.
- If recent history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of price decline), forecast should not continue downward beyond 1–2% below recent low.
- After a sharp spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), forecast should not overcorrect — cap peak correction at 3–5% below spike peak to avoid “overbought” overreaction.
- If sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.5–0.8), forecast should be smoother — avoid sharp directional shifts unless sentiment confirms trend.
- For 30-day horizon, model should not overreact to 1–2 day sentiment swings — lag by 1–2 days to avoid short-term noise amplification.
- If sentiment is consistently high but price is flat or slightly declining, forecast should not assume continuation — expect mean reversion within 3–5 days.
